name: Vocabulary
description: A1/A2 German vocabulary: gender, German→English, and English→German.

items.explanation: Masculine: *der Mann* — most male persons are masculine, no surprise.
Masculine: *der Hund* — most larger animals default to masculine in German.
Masculine: *der Apfel* — fruit names are mostly feminine, but *Apfel* is the classic exception.
Masculine: *der Tisch* — common collocation *am Tisch sitzen* (to sit at the table).
Masculine: *der Stuhl* — pairs with *der Tisch*; plural is *die Stühle* with umlaut.
Masculine: *der Garten* — collocation *im Garten arbeiten* (to work in the garden).
Masculine: days of the week, months, and seasons are all masculine — *der Tag, der Montag, der Sommer*.
Masculine: *der Bruder* — male family members are masculine; plural *die Brüder*.
Masculine: *der Vater* — male family role; plural *die Väter* takes umlaut.
Masculine: *-er* agent nouns are typically masculine — *der Lehrer* = (male) teacher.
Masculine: *der Kaffee* — most hot drinks are masculine (*der Tee*, *der Kakao*).
Masculine: compound takes the gender of its last part — *der Hof* → *der Bahnhof*.
Feminine: *die Frau* — female persons are feminine, no surprise.
Feminine: *die Katze* is the generic word for cat; the male is *der Kater*.
Feminine: most nouns ending in *-e* are feminine — *die Lampe, die Tasche, die Blume*.
Feminine: *die Tür* — collocation *die Tür öffnen / schließen* (to open / close the door).
Feminine: nouns ending in *-e* are typically feminine — *die Straße* (street, road).
Feminine: *-e* ending makes it feminine — *die Schule*; *in die Schule gehen* (to go to school).
Feminine: *die Mutter* — female family role; plural *die Mütter* with umlaut.
Feminine: *die Schwester* — female family member; pairs with *der Bruder*.
Feminine: *die Milch* — just memorize; uncountable in everyday use.
Feminine: *die Uhr* — also used for clock time, as in *Wie viel Uhr ist es?*
Feminine: *-ie* ending is reliably feminine — *die Familie, die Industrie, die Linie*.
Neuter: *das Kind* — children are grammatically neuter regardless of biological sex.
Neuter: *das Buch* — plural *die Bücher* with umlaut and *-er*.
Neuter: *das Auto* — short for *das Automobil*; most *-o* loanwords are neuter.
Neuter: *das Haus* — collocation *nach Hause gehen* (to go home); plural *die Häuser*.
Neuter: *das Brot* — most basic foods just need to be memorized.
Neuter: *das Wasser* — like many liquids and elements, neuter by default.
Neuter: *das Fenster* — exception to the *-er* masculine rule (it is not an agent noun).
Neuter: compound takes gender of the last part — *das Rad* → *das Fahrrad*.
Neuter: *das Hotel* — most foreign loanwords ending in *-el* are neuter.
Noun: *der Apfel* (masculine) — plural *die Äpfel* takes umlaut.
Noun: *das Brot* (neuter) — a *Brötchen* is a small bread roll.
Noun: *der Käse* (masculine) — usually uncountable, like English *cheese*.
Noun: *die Milch* (feminine) — uncountable; collocation *ein Glas Milch*.
Noun: *das Wasser* (neuter) — common request *ein Glas Wasser, bitte*.
Noun: *das Haus* (neuter) — fixed phrase *nach Hause* (toward home).
Noun: *der Tisch* (masculine) — collocation *am Tisch* (at the table).
Noun: *der Stuhl* (masculine) — plural *die Stühle*; contrast with *der Sessel* (armchair).
Noun: *das Buch* (neuter) — plural *die Bücher* with umlaut and *-er*.
Noun: *die Schule* (feminine) — *in die Schule gehen* (to go to school), no article in English idiom.

Noun: *das Fahrrad* (neuter) — informally just *das Rad*.

Strong verb: *sehen → sieht → sah → gesehen*. Contrast with *schauen* (to look).
Strong verb: *essen → isst → aß → gegessen*. For animals use *fressen*.
Strong verb: *trinken → trinkt → trank → getrunken*.
Strong verb: *lesen → liest → las → gelesen*. Vowel changes to *ie* in 2nd/3rd singular.
Strong verb: *schreiben → schrieb → geschrieben*. Takes dative person + accusative thing.
Adjective: *groß* — comparison takes umlaut: *größer / am größten*. Also means *tall* for people.
Adjective: *klein* — regular comparison *kleiner / am kleinsten*; opposite of *groß*.
Adjective: *schön* — also commonly used for *nice / lovely* in everyday speech.
